Pathology-3.question: ১) Philadelphia chromosome is associated with
Pathology-3.exp:
C

The correct answer is CML. The Philadelphia chromosome results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22, designated t(9;22)(q34;q11). This translocation creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. The uncontrolled kinase activity drives excessive proliferation of myeloid cells and is the hallmark of CML.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AML – Philadelphia chromosome is not a characteristic feature, although it is rarely reported in a small subset of cases.

  • ALL – The Philadelphia chromosome may be present, particularly in adult B-cell ALL, but it is not the classical association.

  • CLL – Philadelphia chromosome is not associated with CLL.

High-yield points:

  • Philadelphia chromosome = t(9;22)(q34;q11)

  • Produces the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene with constitutively active tyrosine kinase

  • Classically associated with CML (>90–95% of cases)

  • Also found in a subset of adult ALL, where it indicates a poor prognosis and the need for tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy (e.g., imatinib)

ML is associated with Philadelphia chromosome.

Pathology-3.question: ২) Most common form of Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is nodular sclerosis. It is the most common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, accounting for approximately 60–70% of cases. It typically affects young adults, especially females, and commonly involves the mediastinal and cervical lymph nodes. Histologically, it is characterized by broad collagen bands dividing the lymph node into nodules and the presence of lacunar Reed–Sternberg cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mixed cellularity – The second most common subtype, more frequent in older adults and in patients with HIV infection.

  • Lymphocyte depletion – The least common subtype and is associated with advanced disease and a poorer prognosis.

  • Lymphocyte predominant – An uncommon subtype with characteristic "popcorn" (LP) cells and generally an excellent prognosis.

High-yield points:

  • Most common Hodgkin lymphoma → Nodular sclerosis

  • Most common Reed–Sternberg variant in nodular sclerosis → Lacunar cells

  • Mixed cellularity → Second most common; associated with EBV more frequently

  • Lymphocyte depletion → Least common; worst prognosis

  • Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) → CD20 positive, CD15 and CD30 negative, with LP ("popcorn") cells rather than classical Reed–Sternberg cells

ost common form of Hodgkin’s lymphoma is nodular sclerosing

Pathology-3.question: ৩) Heberden & Bouchard nodes in
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is osteoarthritis (OA). Heberden's nodes are bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, while Bouchard's nodes are bony enlargements of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. They result from osteophyte formation and are characteristic clinical features of osteoarthritis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • RA (Rheumatoid arthritis) – Typically involves the MCP and PIP joints, while the DIP joints are usually spared. Heberden's nodes are not a feature.

  • SLE (Systemic lupus erythematosus) – Causes non-erosive arthritis without Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes.

  • AS (Ankylosing spondylitis) – Primarily affects the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints, not the DIP or PIP joints.

High-yield points:

  • Heberden's nodes → DIP joints → Osteoarthritis

  • Bouchard's nodes → PIP joints → Osteoarthritis

  • RA → MCP and PIP involvement; DIP usually spared

  • OA → Osteophyte formation, joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and bony enlargement

Pathology-3.question: ৪) Von Willebrand factor is synthesised by
Pathology-3.exp:
Vo

The correct answer is endothelial cells. Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is primarily synthesized by vascular endothelial cells and stored in Weibel–Palade bodies. It is also synthesized in megakaryocytes and stored in the α-granules of platelets, but the major source of circulating vWF is the endothelium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Plasma cells – Produce immunoglobulins, not vWF.

  • Subendothelial collagen – Binds vWF after vascular injury but does not synthesize it.

  • Platelets – Store and release vWF from α-granules but are not the primary site of synthesis in standard exam questions.

High-yield points:

  • vWF is synthesized mainly by endothelial cells

  • Also synthesized by megakaryocytes and stored in platelet α-granules

  • Stored in endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies

  • Functions:

    • Mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen (via GpIb)

    • Carries and stabilizes factor VIII

  • von Willebrand disease → ↑Bleeding time, ±↑APTT, normal platelet count

Pathology-3.question: ৫) Benz zones proteinuria
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is multiple myeloma. Bence Jones proteinuria refers to the presence of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) in the urine. These light chains are produced in excess by malignant plasma cells and are a characteristic feature of multiple myeloma. They can cause cast nephropathy (myeloma kidney) and renal impairment.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Leukemia – Does not characteristically produce Bence Jones proteins.

  • Lymphoma – May produce monoclonal proteins rarely, but Bence Jones proteinuria is not a typical feature.

  • Polycythemia – A myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased red cell mass; not associated with Bence Jones proteinuria.

High-yield points:

  • Bence Jones proteins = Free monoclonal κ or λ light chains

  • Most commonly associated with multiple myeloma

  • Detected by urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) and immunofixation

  • Can cause myeloma kidney (cast nephropathy)

  • Multiple myeloma features: CRAB

    • C – HyperCalcaemia

    • R – Renal impairment

    • A – Anaemia

    • B – Bone lesions (lytic lesions/fractures)

Pathology-3.question: ৬) Urine volume can be as low as ... L/day in a dehydrated person?
Pathology-3.exp:
Urine volume can be as low as 0.5 L/day in a dehydrated person or as high as 20 L/day in a person who has been drinking tremendous amounts of water.

The correct answer is 0.5 L/day (500 mL/day). In a dehydrated person, the kidneys conserve water by producing maximally concentrated urine under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). The minimum obligatory urine volume required to excrete daily solute load is approximately 500 mL/day in a healthy adult.

The other options are incorrect because:

1.0 L/day – Higher than the minimum obligatory urine volume.
1.5 L/day – Typical urine output in a well-hydrated adult, not the minimum.
2.0 L/day – Normal urine output with generous fluid intake.
High-yield points:

Minimum obligatory urine volume ≈ 500 mL/day (0.5 L/day)
Normal adult urine output: 0.8–2.0 L/day
Oliguria = <400–500 mL/day
Anuria = <100 mL/day
Polyuria = >3 L/day

Pathology-3.question: ৭) Hypersensitivity in TB
Pathology-3.exp:
Infection typically leads to the development of delayed hypersensitivity to M. tuberculosis antigens, which can be detected by the tuberculin (PPD, or Mantoux) skin test.

The correct answer is Type IV hypersensitivity. The immune response in tuberculosis (TB) is predominantly cell-mediated immunity mediated by T lymphocytes (Th1 cells) and macrophages. Following exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sensitized T cells release cytokines, particularly interferon-γ (IFN-γ), leading to macrophage activation and granuloma formation. This is a delayed-type (48–72 hours) hypersensitivity reaction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Type I – Immediate, IgE-mediated (e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma).

  • Type II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia).

  • Type III – Immune complex-mediated reaction (e.g., serum sickness, SLE).

High-yield points:

  • TB hypersensitivity → Type IV (Delayed)

  • Mediated by Th1 cells and macrophages

  • Key cytokine: IFN-γ

  • Causes granuloma formation and caseous necrosis

  • Mantoux (Tuberculin skin) test is also a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

Pathology-3.question: ৮) Limiting pH of urine
Pathology-3.exp:
The limiting pH of urine is 4.5 .

The correct answer is 4.5. The lowest (limiting) urine pH that the human kidney can produce is approximately 4.5. This reflects the kidney's maximum ability to secrete hydrogen ions (H⁺) into the urine while maintaining acid–base balance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 3.5 – Lower than the physiological minimum; the kidney cannot acidify urine to this level.

  • 4.0 – Also below the normal limiting urine pH.

  • 5.0 – Acidic, but not the lowest achievable urine pH.

High-yield points:

  • Normal urine pH: 4.5–8.0

  • Lowest (minimum) urine pH: 4.5

  • Highest urine pH: ~8.0

  • Acidic urine: Metabolic acidosis, high-protein diet

  • Alkaline urine: UTI with urease-producing organisms, vomiting, vegetarian diet, renal tubular acidosis (Type I)

Pathology-3.question: ৯) Presence of which particle in urine indicates UTI?
Pathology-3.exp:
Presence of nitrite in urine indicates presence of bacteria in urine since some bacteria convert nitrate into nitrite in urine.

The correct answer is nitrite. Many Gram-negative bacteria causing urinary tract infections (especially Escherichia coli) reduce urinary nitrate to nitrite. Therefore, a positive nitrite test on urine dipstick strongly suggests a bacterial UTI.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glucose – Suggests glycosuria (e.g., diabetes mellitus), not UTI.

  • Protein – May occur in many renal diseases and even transiently; not specific for UTI.

  • Bile salts – Indicate hepatobiliary disease, not UTI.

High-yield points:

  • Nitrite-positive urine → Suggests Gram-negative UTI (especially E. coli)

  • Leukocyte esterase → Indicates pyuria and supports UTI

  • Some organisms do not produce nitrite, e.g.:

    • Enterococcus

    • Staphylococcus saprophyticus

    • Pseudomonas (may be variable)

  • Nitrite + Leukocyte esterase together have a high predictive value for UTI.

Pathology-3.question: ১০) Most frequent presentation of extra-pulmonary TB
Pathology-3.exp:
Lymphadenitis is the most frequent presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, usually occurring in the cervical region (“scrofula”).

The correct answer is lymphadenitis. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is the most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB), particularly involving the cervical lymph nodes (scrofula). Patients typically present with chronic, painless lymph node enlargement, which may later become matted or form a sinus.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Paraneoplastic syndrome – Not a manifestation of TB.

  • Vasculitis – Uncommon and not the usual presentation of EPTB.

  • Sacroiliitis – A rare form of skeletal TB; Pott disease (spinal TB) is much more common than sacroiliac involvement.

High-yield points:

  • Most common extrapulmonary TB: Lymphadenitis

  • Most common site: Cervical lymph nodes (scrofula)

  • Other EPTB sites:

    • Pleura

    • Lymph nodes

    • CNS (TB meningitis)

    • Bones and joints (especially spine/Pott disease)

    • Genitourinary tract

    • Peritoneum

Pathology-3.question: ১১) Most common organism in CAP
Pathology-3.exp:
S. pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is the most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia; the distribution of inflammation is usually

The correct answer is Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus). It is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) worldwide in adults and remains the leading bacterial pathogen despite widespread vaccination.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae – Causes CAP mainly in alcoholics, diabetics, and debilitated patients; not the most common.

  • Legionella pneumophila – Causes atypical pneumonia, often associated with contaminated water systems.

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Usually causes hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) or pneumonia in patients with structural lung disease or immunocompromise.

High-yield points:

  • Most common cause of CAP: Streptococcus pneumoniae

  • Typical pathogens: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis

  • Atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella

  • Pseudomonas → HAP, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis

  • Klebsiella → Alcoholics, aspiration risk, "currant jelly" sputum

lobar.

Pathology-3.question: ১২) Pathognomonic for acute rheumatic fever
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Aschoff nodules (Aschoff bodies). They are the pathognomonic histopathological lesion of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). These are granulomatous lesions found in the myocardium, consisting of Anitschkow ("caterpillar") cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and fibrinoid necrosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pericarditis – Can occur in ARF but is not pathognomonic.

  • Pancarditis – A characteristic feature of ARF involving the endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium, but not pathognomonic.

  • Fibrinoid degeneration – Seen in several inflammatory diseases and is not specific to ARF.

High-yield points:

  • Pathognomonic lesion of ARF: Aschoff bodies

  • Characteristic cardiac involvement: Pancarditis

  • Diagnostic criteria: Modified Jones criteria

  • Characteristic cell: Anitschkow ("caterpillar") cell

  • Common chronic sequela: Mitral stenosis due to rheumatic heart disease.

Pathology-3.question: ১৩) Most common cause of angina pectoris
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is atherosclerosis. Angina pectoris is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries, leading to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, especially during exertion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thrombosis – Usually causes acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or myocardial infarction) rather than chronic stable angina.

  • Hyperlipidaemia – A risk factor for atherosclerosis, not the direct cause of angina.

  • Hypertension (HTN) – Also a risk factor that increases myocardial oxygen demand but is not the most common direct cause.

High-yield points:

  • Most common cause of stable angina: Coronary atherosclerosis

  • Stable angina: Fixed ≥70% coronary artery stenosis

  • Unstable angina: Usually due to plaque rupture with non-occlusive thrombosis

Pathology-3.question: ১৪) Which organism is found in pneumonia after organ transplant recipient?
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Legionella. Organ transplant recipients are immunosuppressed and are at increased risk of Legionella pneumophila pneumonia, an important cause of severe atypical pneumonia in this population.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Klebsiella – Causes pneumonia, particularly in alcoholics and hospitalized patients, but is not the classic organism associated with organ transplant recipients.

  • Neisseria – Not a common cause of pneumonia in transplant patients.

  • Pseudomonas – Can cause pneumonia in hospitalized or severely immunocompromised patients, but Legionella is the classic association in transplant recipients in exam questions.

High-yield points:

  • Organ transplant recipient + pneumonia → Think Legionella

  • Risk factors: Immunosuppression, corticosteroid therapy, transplantation

  • Features: High fever, dry cough, hyponatraemia, diarrhea

  • Diagnosis: Urinary Legionella antigen, PCR, culture on BCYE (buffered charcoal yeast extract) agar

  • Treatment: Azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (e.g., levofloxacin)

Pathology-3.question: ১৫) Which lung cancer is common in women?
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is adenocarcinoma. It is the most common type of lung cancer in women, as well as in non-smokers. It usually arises peripherally in the lung and is associated with mutations such as EGFR and ALK.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma – More common in male smokers; typically central in location.

  • Small cell carcinoma – Strongly associated with heavy smoking and usually central.

  • Large cell carcinoma – Less common and can occur anywhere in the lung.

High-yield points:

  • Most common lung cancer overall: Adenocarcinoma

  • Most common in women: Adenocarcinoma

  • Most common in non-smokers: Adenocarcinoma

  • Peripheral lung lesion

  • Common mutations: EGFR, ALK, KRAS

  • Squamous cell carcinoma → Hypercalcaemia (↑PTHrP)

  • Small cell carcinoma → SIADH, ACTH, Lambert–Eaton syndrome

Pathology-3.question: ১৬) Most common primary cardiac tumour in adults
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is myxoma. It is the most common primary cardiac tumour in adults. About 75% arise in the left atrium, usually from the interatrial septum (fossa ovalis), and may present with mitral valve obstruction, embolic events, or constitutional symptoms.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Myeloma – A plasma cell malignancy of the bone marrow, not a primary cardiac tumour.

  • Rhabdomyoma – Most common primary cardiac tumour in children, especially associated with tuberous sclerosis.

  • Sarcoma – The most common primary malignant cardiac tumour in adults, but not the most common primary cardiac tumour overall.

High-yield points:

  • Most common primary cardiac tumour (adults): Myxoma

  • Most common primary malignant cardiac tumour (adults): Sarcoma (especially angiosarcoma)

  • Most common cardiac tumour overall: Metastatic tumours

  • Most common primary cardiac tumour in children: Rhabdomyoma

Pathology-3.question: ১৭) Most common cause of acute infective endocarditis
Pathology-3.exp:
Reference: Davidson 23rd; P-528

The correct answer is Staphylococcus aureus. It is the most common cause of acute infective endocarditis, producing a rapidly destructive infection that can affect both normal and abnormal valves.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Viridans streptococci – Most common cause of subacute infective endocarditis on previously damaged valves.

  • Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) – Associated with infective endocarditis and colorectal carcinoma, but not the most common cause of acute IE.

  • Enterococci – Common after genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures, especially in elderly patients.

High-yield points:

  • Acute infective endocarditis: Staphylococcus aureus

  • Subacute infective endocarditis: Viridans streptococci

  • IV drug users: S. aureus (often tricuspid valve)

  • S. gallolyticus endocarditis → Screen for colorectal cancer

  • Prosthetic valve (<1 year): Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause.

Pathology-3.question: ১৮) Mechanism of heart failure following MI
Pathology-3.exp:
Reference: Davidson 23rd; P-462

The correct answer is reduced ventricular contractility. Following myocardial infarction (MI), necrosis of the myocardium leads to loss of functioning cardiac muscle, resulting in decreased left ventricular systolic contractility, reduced cardiac output, and ultimately heart failure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ventricular outflow obstruction – Seen in conditions like aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not typical after MI.

  • Ventricular inflow obstruction – Occurs in mitral stenosis or atrial tumors, not due to MI.

  • Ventricular volume overload – May occur if MI causes papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation, but this is a complication, not the usual mechanism of heart failure after MI.

High-yield points:

  • Most common mechanism of HF after MI: Reduced ventricular contractility (LV systolic dysfunction)

  • Large anterior MI → Highest risk of heart failure

  • Acute mechanical complications: Papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture, free wall rupture

  • Reduced ejection fraction is typical after extensive MI.

Pathology-3.question: ১৯) Most common congenital cardiac malformation
Pathology-3.exp:
Reference: Davidson 23rd; P-531

The correct answer is Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD). It is the most common congenital cardiac malformation (excluding bicuspid aortic valve) and the most common congenital heart disease at birth. Most VSDs occur in the membranous septum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ASD – Common in adults due to late diagnosis but less common than VSD at birth.

  • PDA – Common in premature infants but not the most common congenital cardiac malformation overall.

  • TOF – The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond the neonatal period, but not the most common congenital heart defect overall.

High-yield points:

  • Most common congenital cardiac malformation: VSD

  • Most common cyanotic CHD (overall): Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)

  • Most common cyanotic CHD after the neonatal period: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

  • Most common congenital heart disease in adults: ASD (due to survival into adulthood)

Pathology-3.question: ২০) Which of the following is called “cardiac asthma”?
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND). Cardiac asthma refers to wheezing and breathlessness caused by left ventricular failure, typically presenting as PND due to pulmonary congestion and bronchial mucosal edema. It is not bronchial asthma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Orthopnea – Breathlessness occurring on lying flat, relieved by sitting up.

  • Platypnea – Breathlessness worse in the upright position, relieved by lying down.

  • Trepopnea – Breathlessness occurring in one lateral decubitus position but not the other.

High-yield points:

  • Cardiac asthma = PND due to left heart failure

  • PND: Awakens the patient 2–4 hours after sleep with severe dyspnea

  • Orthopnea: Dyspnea immediately on lying flat

  • Platypnea: Worse when standing/sitting (e.g., hepatopulmonary syndrome)

  • Trepopnea: Dyspnea in one lateral position (e.g., unilateral lung disease or heart failure)

Pathology-3.question: ২১) What is the most common cause of aortic aneurysm?
Pathology-3.exp:
Reference: Davidson 23rd , Page : 505

The correct answer is atherosclerosis. It is the most common cause of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), the commonest type of aortic aneurysm. Atherosclerosis weakens the aortic wall, leading to progressive dilatation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hyperlipidaemia – A risk factor for atherosclerosis, not the direct cause.

  • Hypertension – A major risk factor, especially for aortic dissection, but not the most common cause of aneurysm.

  • Diabetes mellitus – Not a common cause of aortic aneurysm and is paradoxically associated with a lower prevalence of AAA.

High-yield points:

  • Most common cause of aortic aneurysm (especially AAA): Atherosclerosis

  • Most common cause of thoracic aortic aneurysm: Hypertension (with medial degeneration)

  • Major risk factors for AAA: Smoking, male sex, age >65 years, atherosclerosis

  • Hypertension is the most important risk factor for aortic dissection.

Pathology-3.question: ২২) Mumps usually infects
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is parotid gland. Mumps virus (a paramyxovirus) most commonly causes acute parotitis, affecting one or both parotid glands.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sublingual gland – Rarely involved.

  • Submandibular gland – May occasionally be affected but much less commonly than the parotid gland.

  • Buccal gland – Not a typical site of mumps infection.

High-yield points:

  • Most commonly affected salivary gland: Parotid gland

  • Causative organism: Mumps virus (Paramyxovirus)

  • Complications: Orchitis, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, oophoritis, sensorineural hearing loss

  • Prevention: MMR vaccine

Pathology-3.question: ২৩) Most common tumor of the salivary gland
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Pleomorphic adenoma. It is the most common salivary gland tumour and the most common benign salivary gland tumour, most frequently arising in the parotid gland.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Adenocarcinoma – Malignant but uncommon.

  • Warthin tumour – Second most common benign parotid tumour, strongly associated with smoking.

  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma – Most common malignant salivary gland tumour, but not the most common overall.

High-yield points:

  • Most common salivary gland tumour: Pleomorphic adenoma

  • Most common benign salivary gland tumour: Pleomorphic adenoma

  • Most common malignant salivary gland tumour: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma

  • Most common site: Parotid gland

  • Pleomorphic adenoma has a risk of malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) if long-standing.

Pathology-3.question: ২৪) Disease that allows “selective” loss of albumin is?
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Minimal change disease (MCD). It causes selective proteinuria, with predominant loss of albumin, due to podocyte foot process effacement while the glomerular basement membrane remains structurally intact.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Diabetes – Causes non-selective proteinuria as nephropathy progresses.

  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) – Typically causes non-selective proteinuria, including larger plasma proteins.

  • Hypertension – May cause mild proteinuria but not selective albumin loss.

High-yield points:

  • Selective albuminuria: Minimal change disease

  • Electron microscopy: Foot process effacement

  • Light microscopy: Usually normal

  • Steroid response: Excellent (especially in children)

  • FSGS and membranous nephropathy: Usually non-selective proteinuria

Pathology-3.question: ২৫) Most important risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Barrett's oesophagus. It is the most important premalignant condition and the strongest risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) leads to intestinal metaplasia of the distal oesophagus, which can progress to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Achalasia cardia – Predisposes mainly to oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

  • Mallory–Weiss tear – A mucosal tear causing upper GI bleeding; not premalignant.

  • Oesophageal fistula – Not a recognized risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

High-yield points:

  • Most important risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma: Barrett's oesophagus

  • Major underlying cause: Chronic GERD

  • Adenocarcinoma: Usually lower one-third of the oesophagus

  • Squamous cell carcinoma: Associated with smoking, alcohol, achalasia, caustic injury; usually middle one-third of the oesophagus.

Pathology-3.question: ২৬) Most common site of carcinoid tumor-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is the vermiform appendix. It is the most common site of gastrointestinal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumours in standard undergraduate and FCPS examinations. Most appendiceal carcinoids are discovered incidentally during appendicectomy and have an excellent prognosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Small intestine (especially terminal ileum) – A common site and the most common site of malignant carcinoid tumours, but not the most common overall.

  • Rectum – A common site but less frequent than the appendix.

  • Stomach – Less common.

High-yield points:

  • Most common site of carcinoid tumour: Appendix

  • Most common malignant GI carcinoid: Terminal ileum

  • Carcinoid syndrome: Usually occurs with liver metastasis

  • Carcinoid syndrome features: Flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular heart disease

  • Biochemical marker: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA

Pathology-3.question: ২৭) Morphological pictures of peptic ulcer-
Pathology-3.option1: ক) Superficial thin layer of granulation tissue
Pathology-3.option3: গ) Superficial layer of necrotic debris
Pathology-3.exp:
Bence Jones proteinuria refers to the excretion of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) in the urine. These light chains are synthesized in excess by malignant plasma cells, making this a classic hallmark of Multiple Myeloma.

  • Multiple Myeloma (ঘ) — Correct: Proliferation of neoplastic plasma cells produces excess light chains that pass through the glomerulus into the urine, often causing cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney").

  • Leukemia (ক): A malignancy of blood-forming tissue/white blood cells; not typically associated with Bence Jones light chains.

  • Lymphoma (খ): A malignancy of the lymphatic system; light chain proteinuria is not a characteristic feature.

  • Polycythemia (গ): A myeloproliferative disorder leading to elevated red blood cell mass; unrelated to Bence Jones proteins.

Pathology-3.question: ২৮) Urinary bladder cancer caused by-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Schistosoma haematobium. Chronic infection with S. haematobium causes persistent inflammation, squamous metaplasia, and is strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

The other options are incorrect because:

Gonococcal infection – Causes urethritis and PID, not bladder cancer.
Chlamydial infection – Causes urethritis and genital infections, not bladder cancer.
Schistosoma mansoni – Primarily affects the intestine and liver, not the urinary bladder.
High-yield points:

Bladder cancer associated with Schistosoma: S. haematobium
Histological type: Squamous cell carcinoma
Most common bladder cancer worldwide: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma
Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma: Smoking, aromatic amines, cyclophosphamide, pelvic irradiation.

Pathology-3.question: ২৯) Malignant tumor of urethrae -
Pathology-3.exp:
The most common malignant tumour of the urethra is urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, particularly in the proximal urethra, where the lining is urothelial.

The other options:

  • ক) Squamous cell papilloma – Benign epithelial tumour.

  • খ) Transitional cell papilloma – Benign urothelial tumour.

  • গ) Adenocarcinoma – Malignant, but uncommon; may arise from periurethral glands or urethral diverticula.

High-yield points:

  • Most common urethral malignancy: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma

  • Distal urethra: More commonly squamous cell carcinoma

  • Female urethral diverticulum: Predisposes to adenocarcinoma

  • Papillomas are benign, whereas carcinomas are malignant.

Pathology-3.question: ৩০) Interstitial disease of kidney -
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Pyelonephritis, which is an interstitial (tubulointerstitial) disease of the kidney. It primarily involves the renal interstitium and tubules, usually due to a bacterial infection.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Glomerulonephritis – A glomerular disease.

  • গ) Nephrotic syndrome – A clinical syndrome resulting from glomerular diseases, not an interstitial disease.

  • ঘ) Polycystic kidney disease – A hereditary cystic disease of the kidney, not classified as an interstitial disease.

High-yield points:

  • Tubulointerstitial diseases: Acute pyelonephritis, Chronic pyelonephritis, Acute interstitial nephritis

  • Glomerular diseases: Glomerulonephritis, Nephrotic syndrome

  • Cystic disease: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

  • Acute pyelonephritis: Neutrophilic infiltration of the interstitium and tubules (tubulointerstitial nephritis).

Pathology-3.question: ৩১) Most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Minimal Change Disease (MCD). It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, accounting for about 80–90% of cases in children younger than 10 years. It is characterized by diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy and typically shows an excellent response to corticosteroids.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Membranous glomerulopathy – More common in adults.

  • গ) IgA nephropathy – The most common glomerulonephritis worldwide; usually presents with nephritic syndrome (recurrent hematuria), not nephrotic syndrome.

  • ঘ) Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) – An important cause of nephrotic syndrome, especially in adults and steroid-resistant children, but not the most common in children.

High-yield points:

  • Most common nephrotic syndrome in children: Minimal Change Disease

  • Most common nephrotic syndrome in adults: Membranous nephropathy (many exam references) / FSGS is increasingly common in some populations.

  • Light microscopy (MCD): Normal glomeruli

  • Electron microscopy: Diffuse foot process effacement

  • Immunofluorescence: Negative

  • Response to steroids: Excellent

Pathology-3.question: ৩২) Neuronal tumor of CNS-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Gangliocytoma, which is a neuronal tumour of the central nervous system composed of mature ganglion cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Astrocytoma – A glial tumour arising from astrocytes.

  • গ) Schwannoma – A peripheral nerve sheath tumour arising from Schwann cells (not a CNS neuronal tumour).

  • ঘ) Medulloblastoma – An embryonal neuroepithelial tumour, not classified as a mature neuronal tumour.

High-yield points:

  • Neuronal tumours: Gangliocytoma, Ganglioglioma, Central neurocytoma

  • Glial tumours: Astrocytoma, Oligodendroglioma, Ependymoma

  • Peripheral nerve sheath tumour: Schwannoma

  • Medulloblastoma: Malignant embryonal tumour of the cerebellum, common in children.

Pathology-3.question: ৩৩) Commonest glial tumor-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Astrocytoma, which is the most common glial tumour of the central nervous system. Astrocytomas range from WHO Grade 1 (pilocytic astrocytoma) to WHO Grade 4 (glioblastoma).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Oligodendroglioma – Less common glial tumour, often associated with 1p/19q codeletion and IDH mutation.

  • গ) Ependymoma – Arises from ependymal cells, commonly in the fourth ventricle in children.

  • ঘ) Ganglioglioma – A rare mixed neuronal-glial tumour, not the commonest glial tumour.

High-yield points:

  • Most common glial tumour: Astrocytoma

  • Most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults: Glioblastoma (Grade 4 astrocytoma)

  • Most common benign brain tumour: Meningioma

  • Most common primary brain tumour overall: Meningioma

  • Most common paediatric brain tumour: Pilocytic astrocytoma

  • Most common malignant paediatric brain tumour: Medulloblastoma

Pathology-3.question: ৩৪) Childhood tumor occurs in cerebellum -
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Medulloblastoma. It is the most common malignant brain tumour of childhood and typically arises in the cerebellum, usually from the midline cerebellar vermis. It is a highly malignant embryonal (WHO Grade 4) tumour with a tendency to spread via the CSF ("drop metastases").

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Astrocytoma – Pilocytic astrocytoma also occurs in the cerebellum of children but is benign (WHO Grade 1) and is not the classic malignant childhood cerebellar tumour.

  • গ) Oligodendroglioma – Usually occurs in the cerebral hemispheres of adults.

  • ঘ) Meningioma – Arises from the meninges, mainly in adults.

High-yield points:

  • Most common malignant cerebellar tumour in children: Medulloblastoma

  • Most common benign cerebellar tumour in children: Pilocytic astrocytoma

  • Location: Cerebellar vermis (midline)

  • Spread: CSF dissemination ("drop metastases")

  • Histology: Small round blue cell tumour

Pathology-3.question: ৩৫) CSF glucose is characteristically reduced in all of the following except:
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Viral meningitis because CSF glucose is usually normal in viral meningitis. In contrast, acute bacterial (pyogenic), tuberculous, and fungal meningitis characteristically cause reduced CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) due to increased glucose consumption by microorganisms and inflammatory cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Acute bacterial meningitis – CSF glucose decreased.

  • খ) Tuberculous meningitis – CSF glucose decreased.

  • গ) Fungal meningitis – CSF glucose decreased.

High-yield points:

Type of meningitis CSF Glucose
Acute bacterial (pyogenic) ↓↓↓
Tuberculous ↓
Fungal ↓
Viral Normal

Rapid recall:
"Low glucose = Bacterial, TB, Fungal; Normal glucose = Viral."

Pathology-3.question: ৩৬) Degenerative disease affecting cerebral cortex-
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Alzheimer's disease, which is the most common degenerative disease affecting the cerebral cortex. It is a cortical neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive impairment of memory, cognition, language, and executive function.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Parkinson's disease – Primarily affects the substantia nigra (basal ganglia).

  • খ) Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) – A brainstem and basal ganglia tauopathy.

  • ঘ) Corticobasal degeneration – Involves both the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia, but is much less common and not the classic cortical degenerative disease.

High-yield points:

  • Most common cortical degenerative disease: Alzheimer's disease

  • Pathology: β-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau)

  • Most affected regions: Hippocampus and cerebral cortex

  • Parkinson disease: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

Pathology-3.question: ৩৭) Gastric metastasis to pouch of Doglas is known as
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Blumer shelf, which refers to a metastatic deposit in the rectovesical pouch (male) or pouch of Douglas (female), classically from gastric carcinoma. On rectal examination, it may be felt as a hard shelf-like mass.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Irish node – Left axillary lymph node metastasis from gastric carcinoma.

  • খ) Virchow gland (Virchow node) – Left supraclavicular lymph node metastasis (Troisier sign).

  • ঘ) Sister Mary Joseph nodule – Umbilical metastatic nodule from intra-abdominal malignancies, especially gastric carcinoma.

High-yield points:

  • Pouch of Douglas metastasis: Blumer shelf

  • Left supraclavicular node: Virchow node

  • Left axillary node: Irish node

  • Umbilical metastasis: Sister Mary Joseph nodule

  • Bilateral ovarian metastasis from gastric carcinoma: Krukenberg tumour

Pathology-3.question: ৩৮) Most gastric adenocarcinoma involves
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Antrum. Classically, the most common site of gastric adenocarcinoma is the antrum, particularly along the lesser curvature near the pylorus. This is the standard answer in pathology and FCPS/MBBS examinations.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Cardia – The incidence is increasing in Western countries, but it is not the classic most common site in standard pathology exams.

  • গ) Pylorus – May be involved, but less commonly than the antrum/lesser curvature.

  • ঘ) Body – Less common.

High-yield points:

  • Most common site of gastric adenocarcinoma (exam): Antrum (lesser curvature)

  • Most common histological type: Adenocarcinoma

  • Lauren classification: Intestinal type and Diffuse type

  • Major risk factors: Helicobacter pylori, chronic atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, smoking, high-salt diet, nitrosamines.

Pathology-3.question: ৩৯) Common site of local invasion of gastric carcinoma excludes
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Jejunum because it is not a common site of direct local invasion by gastric carcinoma.

Common sites of local extension of gastric carcinoma include:

  • ক) Duodenum — ✅ Common

  • গ) Pancreas — ✅ Common (especially posterior gastric wall tumors)

  • ঘ) Retroperitoneum — ✅ Can be involved by advanced posterior extension

The jejunum is anatomically distant from the stomach and is not a usual site of direct invasion.

High-yield points:

  • Common local invasion: Duodenum, pancreas, transverse colon, omentum, liver, retroperitoneum

  • Lymphatic spread: Virchow node

  • Transcoelomic spread: Blumer shelf, Krukenberg tumour

  • Umbilical metastasis: Sister Mary Joseph nodule

Pathology-3.question: ৪০) Intranasal cocaine users are at risk of which hepatitis virus
৪১) Ground glass cells are found in chronic infection with hepatitis
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Hepatitis B. Ground-glass hepatocytes are a characteristic histological feature of chronic hepatitis B infection. They result from the accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) within the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes, giving the cytoplasm a homogeneous, finely granular "ground-glass" appearance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Hepatitis C – Characterized by lymphoid aggregates and hepatic steatosis, not ground-glass cells.

  • গ) Hepatitis D – Occurs only with HBV but ground-glass hepatocytes are due to HBsAg of HBV, not HDV itself.

  • ঘ) Hepatitis E – Does not produce ground-glass hepatocytes.

High-yield points:

  • Ground-glass hepatocytes → Chronic Hepatitis B (HBsAg accumulation)

  • Hepatitis C: Lymphoid follicles, steatosis

  • HBV marker in hepatocytes: HBsAg

  • HBV can lead to: Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

Pathology-3.question: ৪২) The inflammatory cell in both acute & chronic viral hepatitis mainly
৪৩) Recurrent hematuria is a most frequent clinical presentation of
৪৪) Most common infective agent in acute pyelonephritis
৪৫) Focal cerebral infarcts are most commonly
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Embolic. Focal cerebral infarcts are most commonly caused by arterial emboli, which usually originate from the heart (e.g., atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, infective endocarditis) or from atheromatous plaques in the carotid arteries.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Inflammatory – Vasculitis can cause infarction but is uncommon.

  • খ) Neoplastic – Tumors cause mass effect rather than focal infarction.

  • গ) Traumatic – Trauma may cause hemorrhage or contusion, not the common cause of focal cerebral infarction.

High-yield points:

  • Most common cause of focal cerebral infarct: Embolism

  • Most common source of emboli: Heart (especially atrial fibrillation)

  • Watershed infarcts: Due to systemic hypotension

  • Lacunar infarcts: Due to lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries in hypertension

Pathology-3.question: ৪৬) Type of hypersensitivity in SLE
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Type III hypersensitivity. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is primarily an immune complex-mediated disease. Antigen-antibody (Ag-Ab) immune complexes deposit in tissues (e.g., kidneys, skin, joints, blood vessels), activate the complement system, and cause inflammation and tissue damage.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Type I – IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma).

  • খ) Type II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome). Although some manifestations of SLE (e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia) are Type II, the overall disease mechanism is Type III.

  • ঘ) Type IV – T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity (e.g., contact dermatitis, tuberculosis).

High-yield points:

  • SLE: Type III hypersensitivity

  • Mechanism: Immune complex deposition → Complement activation → Inflammation

  • Complement levels: C3 and C4 are decreased during active disease

  • Type II manifestations in SLE: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia (important exam point)

Pathology-3.question: ৪৭) Radiographic hallmarks in RA excludes
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Widening of the joint space, because it is not a radiographic hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

Typical radiographic features of RA include:

  • ক) Joint effusions – ✅ May be seen as soft tissue swelling early in the disease.

  • খ) Juxta-articular osteopenia with erosions – ✅ Characteristic feature of RA.

  • ঘ) Loss of articular cartilage – ✅ Leads to joint space narrowing, not widening.

Joint space widening is not a feature of RA; instead, RA causes progressive, uniform joint space narrowing due to cartilage destruction.

High-yield points:

  • Early X-ray findings: Soft tissue swelling, juxta-articular osteopenia

  • Characteristic finding: Marginal erosions

  • Joint space: Uniform narrowing

  • Late changes: Deformities, subluxation, ankylosis (occasionally)

  • Osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis: Typical of osteoarthritis, not RA.

Pathology-3.question: ৪৮) Required plasma level(minimum) for development of gout
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is 6.8 mg/dL, which is the physiological saturation point of monosodium urate in plasma at 37°C. Above this level, monosodium urate crystals can precipitate in joints and tissues, predisposing to gout. However, not everyone with hyperuricemia develops gout.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) 5.8 mg/dL – Below the saturation threshold.

  • গ) 7.8 mg/dL – Hyperuricemia, but crystal formation begins at a lower level.

  • ঘ) 9.8 mg/dL – Increases the risk further but is not the minimum required level.

High-yield points:

  • Minimum plasma urate level for crystal formation: 6.8 mg/dL (≈404 μmol/L)

  • Definitive diagnosis of gout: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid

  • Most commonly affected joint: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra)

  • Chronic gout: Tophi, erosive arthritis, uric acid nephrolithiasis

Pathology-3.question: ৪৯) Pathognomonic hallmark of gout
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Tophi. Tophi are the pathognomonic hallmark of chronic gout. They are nodular deposits of monosodium urate crystals surrounded by a foreign-body giant cell granulomatous reaction, typically found in the ear pinna, olecranon, Achilles tendon, fingers, and toes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Acute arthritis – Common presentation but not pathognomonic.

  • খ) Chronic tophaceous arthritis – Represents advanced gout, but the pathognomonic lesion is the tophus itself.

  • ঘ) Gouty nephropathy – A complication, not the defining hallmark.

High-yield points:

  • Pathognomonic lesion of gout: Tophus (Tophi)

  • Composition: Monosodium urate crystals with foreign-body giant cell reaction

  • Definitive diagnosis: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid

  • Most commonly affected joint: First MTP joint (podagra)

  • Tophi indicate: Chronic gout

Pathology-3.question: ৫০) Most common type of joint disease
Pathology-3.exp:
The correct answer is Osteoarthritis (OA). It is the most common joint disease worldwide, characterized by progressive degeneration of articular cartilage, subchondral bone remodeling, osteophyte formation, and varying degrees of synovial inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Osteoporosis – A metabolic bone disease, not a joint disease.

  • গ) Osteomalacia – Defective bone mineralization; a bone disorder, not a joint disease.

  • ঘ) Osteonecrosis – Ischemic necrosis of bone; less common and not primarily a joint disease.

High-yield points:

  • Most common joint disease: Osteoarthritis

  • Most commonly affected joints: Knees, hips, hands (DIP > PIP), cervical and lumbar spine

  • Radiographic features: Joint space narrowing (non-uniform), osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts

  • Heberden nodes: DIP joints

  • Bouchard nodes: PIP joints
